Amplias
AM-plee-as
proper noun
Latin Amplias, a shortened form of Ampliatus, “enlarged” or “extended,” a believer at Rome whom Paul calls his beloved.

📖 Biblical Definition

Amplias is named but once in all of Scripture, in the long roll of greetings that closes the epistle to the Romans: “Greet Amplias my beloved in the Lord” (Rom 16:8). Nothing more is told of him; we know not his station, his labours, nor his end. Yet the few words that name him are weighty beyond measure, for the great apostle calls him “my beloved in the Lord.” His name, a common one borne often by servants and freedmen of the Roman household, suggests a man of humble or even servile rank; and it is striking that the gospel had so knit this obscure man to Paul that the apostle should send him a personal salutation across the sea. Here is the communion of saints in its sweetness: a bond of love in the Lord that crosses every barrier of rank and distance, and that the Holy Ghost saw fit to set down forever in the inspired record. Amplias stands as a witness that Christ knows His own by name, however unknown they may be to the world; that the least and lowliest of believers is precious to the saints and to the Saviour; and that to be “beloved in the Lord” is a higher honour than any the world can give. His name is written in Scripture, and, what is more, in the Lamb’s book of life.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A believer at Rome, named once, whom Paul greets as “my beloved in the Lord” (Rom 16:8).

AMPLIAS, a believer at Rome greeted by Paul (Rom 16:8).

Paul calls him “my beloved in the Lord.”

His name is a shortened form of Ampliatus.

It was a name common among servants and freedmen of Rome.

Nothing more of him is recorded in Scripture.

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 16:8 — "Greet Amplias my beloved in the Lord."

Rom 16:5 — "Likewise greet the church that is in their house. Salute my wellbeloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ."

Rom 16:9 — "Salute Urbane, our helper in Christ, and Stachys my beloved."

1Co 1:27 — "But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A saint of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; he witnesses to the dignity of the obscure believer beloved in the Lord.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of the obscure believer who is beloved in the Lord. Amplias is named once, and nothing of his deeds survives; yet the great apostle calls him “my beloved,” and the Holy Ghost set the greeting in the eternal record. The communion of saints crosses every barrier of rank and distance; the lowliest believer, perhaps a servant of the Roman household, is precious to the saints and to the Saviour.

Amplias also witnesses that Christ knows His own by name, however unknown they are to the world. A man whose whole earthly memorial is four words of greeting is remembered forever because he was loved in the Lord. To be beloved in the Lord is a higher honour than any the world can bestow; and the name written so briefly in Romans is, by grace, written also in the Lamb’s book of life, where it shall never be blotted out.
